title: Pull here to slow the climate crisis
content: Methane is a greenhouse gas responsible for roughly a third of today’s global heating, and it may be our best chance to curb the climate crisis. Compared to its better-known sibling carbon dioxide (CO₂), which can stay in the atmosphere for hundreds to thousands of years, methane's lifespan is relatively short at only about 12 years. That gives us a solid chance to slow down the climate crisis, according to the European Civil Society Observatory on Methane (CSO-M), and buy time to deal with CO₂ emissions. But where do we start if we want to hit the methane brake? If you imagine the EU's total methane emissions as a pie of three ingredients, one really is burping cows: the majority still come from agriculture. The second ingredient is organic waste, which releases methane as it breaks down in landfills. The third is fossil fuels. Methane can escape to the air in almost any stage of their life cycle, whether released intentionally or leaked by accident. Methane from the energy sector is also the easiest and most cost-effective to reduce, Maria Olczak, senior research fellow at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, told The European Correspondent. title: “I wish they could pass the bill today”: Ghanaian women accused of being witches on long-awaited legislation
content:
In Ghana, people accused of witchcraft, primarily older women, face threats, physical attacks and in some cases, death. They have no safe place to escape to other than camps in Northern and North-eastern regions overseen by religious leaders, as documented in Amnesty International’s 2025 report.

In 2023, the Anti-Witchcraft Accusations Bill, which seeks to establish a legal framework for addressing accusations of witchcraft and related abuses, including the protection and reintegration of persons affected, was passed by parliament as a private members’ bill. However, it was not signed into law by the then president, who cited constitutional concerns.  

In July 2026, the bill was reintroduced to Ghana’s Parliament as a private members bill. Since September, the government is moving to take over the bill as a government-sponsored bill, aiming to facilitate its passage and implementation. The Minister of Gender confirmed that government was working towards reintegration of camp residents and eventual closure of the camps.

Amnesty International visited three of these camps, in Gambaga, Kukuo and Gnani, in April and May 2026, where six resident women shared their stories and hopes.

title: Amnesty: Gazan syntyvyys laskussa – tutkittava osana Israelin toteuttamaa kansanmurhaa
content:
Amnestyn uusi raportti No Conditions for Life: Women, Girls and the Gendered Dimensions of Israel’s Genocide Against Palestinians in Gaza (liitteenä) tarkastelee Israelin Gazassa toteuttaman kansanmurhan vaikutuksia erityisesti naisiin ja tyttöihin. Israel on vuosina 2023–2026 järjestelmällisesti tappanut, haavoittanut, pakkosiirtänyt ja nälkiinnyttänyt palestiinalaisia naisia ja tyttöjä sekä estänyt heitä saamasta välttämätöntä terveydenhuoltoa. Tämän seurauksena naisten mahdollisuudet tehdä omaa lisääntymisterveyttään, raskautta ja synnytystä koskevia päätöksiä eivät toteudu.

"Amnesty totesi yksiselitteisesti jo kaksi vuotta sitten, että Israel syyllistyy kansanmurhaan Gazassa. Uusi raportti osoittaa, miten syvällisesti kansanmurha on vaikuttanut juuri naisiin ja tyttöihin", sanoo Amnesty Internationalin pääsihteeri Agnès Callamard.

Gazan terveysministeriön mukaan Israel tappoi hyökkäyksillään 7.10.2023–1.10.2026 välillä yhteensä 22 331 naista ja tyttöä. He muodostavat noin 30 prosenttia kaikista kuolonuhreista. Kansanmurhan kahden ensimmäisen vuoden aikana Israel tappoi keskimäärin 30 naista tai tyttöä joka päivä.

title: The Power of the Plenum: Leaderless Student Organising in Serbian and Croatian Student Movements
content:
Explore how leaderless, direct-democratic plenums have worked across student movements from Serbia’s 2026 student blockades to Croatia’s 2009 free-education occupation.

Plenums are open, non-hierarchical discussion and decision-making assemblies where every participant holds an equal voice, enabling movements to make decisions collectively without permanent leaders.

Plenums were used by students in Serbia in 2026, building on precedents such as the 2009 protests in Croatia, when students at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences in Zagreb staged a monthlong occupation. Below is a collection of guides and articles about this decision making model.

If you have practical guides, reflections, or case studies on plenums to suggest please contact us.

A plenum-type gathering is a first-aid kit for patchwork democracy, rooted in the belief that political change from below is possible. – Suzana Ignjatovic

title: Canberra’s pact with Manila offers Brussels lesson in practical defence
content:
Australia has signed a new defence deal with the Philippines. The main takeaway for Europe: practical cooperation can carry more weight than grand declarations.

The Defence Cooperation Arrangement, signed in mid-November, expands an existing memorandum of understanding on defence cooperation. It sets out priorities for maritime awareness, information-sharing, strategic dialogue, planning, training, and interoperability. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese witnessed the signing aboard HMAS Stalwart in Manila.

Mr Albanese framed the deal as part of a wider regional effort. “Australia is committed to working closely with ASEAN to help shape a region that is peaceful, stable and prosperous,” he said. Canberra has also committed to its Southeast Asia Maritime Partnerships, which support practical work with regional partners.

title: Raportti: Lapset saavat vain pienen siivun Suomen kehitysyhteistyörahoituksesta
content:
Suomen kehitysyhteistyörahoituksesta noin viidesosa osoitetaan lapsille. Osuus on viime vuosina kasvanut, mutta se johtuu osin kehitysyhteistyöleikkauksista, kertoo lastenjärjestö Suomen UNICEF tuoreen analyysinsä pohjalta.

Järjestö tutki Suomen kehitysyhteistyörahoitusta vuosina 2014–2024. Sinä aikana paljon on muuttunut: kehitysyhteistyörahoitus nousi huipputasoonsa vuonna 2022 mutta on sen jälkeen laskenut.

Lasten saaman rahoituksen osuus on näinä vuosina kyllä kasvanut muutaman prosenttiyksikön verran. Toisaalta leikkausten vuoksi euromääräinen kasvu on ollut vain 36 miljoonaa euroa, Unicef kertoo.

Yhteensä Suomi antoi vuonna 2024 noin 313 miljoonaa euroa lapsiin kohdistuvaa kehitysyhteistyörahoitusta.

Suomi saa Unicefilta kiitosta erityisesti terveys- ja koulutussektorien rahoituksesta, sillä siitä valtaosa kanavoidaan lapsille. Kumpikin on viime vuosina kuitenkin vähentynyt, lasten koulutusrahoitus peräti 57 prosenttia.

Humanitaarisesta avusta eli kriisien ja katastrofien yhteydessä annettavasta avusta vain 14 prosenttia menee lapsille.

title: Pieni Montenegro on testi EU:n laajentumiskyvylle
content:
EU valmistautuu laajenemaan, ja pisimmälle päässeen ehdokasmaan Montenegron jäsenyysneuvottelut lähestyvät loppusuoraa. Pienikokoinen Balkanin valtio olisi ehdokasmaista kenties helpoin integroida unioniin, mutta prosessi on tuonut esiin monia ongelmia aina uudistusten vauhdista naapurimaan vaatimuksiin ja siihen, miten varmistaa sujuva päätöksenteko entistä laajemmassa unionissa.

Euroopan unionin ehdokasmaiden kärjessä on 620 000 asukkaan Montenegro, joka pyrkii liittymään unionin 28. jäsenmaaksi vuoteen 2028 mennessä. Maan väestöstä 68 % kannattaa EU-jäsenyyttä, ja hallitus vie EU:n vaatimia uudistuksia eteenpäin kovaa vauhtia. 

Marraskuun alussa julkaisemassaan vuotuisessa laajentumispaketissa Euroopan komissio arvioi EU:n ehdokasmaiden tilannetta ja etenemistä jäsenyyspolulla. Komission mukaan Montenegro on suurimmaksi osin toteuttanut jäsenyysneuvotteluissa vaaditut uudistukset, ja neuvottelut voitaisiin saattaa päätökseen jo kuluvan vuoden loppuun mennessä. Tämän jälkeen Montenegron EU-jäsenyys vaatii vielä kaikkien nykyisten jäsenmaiden hyväksynnän.

title: Huawei sai yritysvakoilusta tuomion Yhdysvalloissa
content:
Yhdysvalloissa oikeus on tuominnut kiinalaisen teknologiajätin Huawein liikesalaisuuksien varastamisesta ja hyödyntämisestä.

Tuomio annettiin tiistaina liittovaltion tuomioistuimessa viikkoja kestäneen oikeudenkäynnin päätteeksi.

Laitevalmistajaa syytettiin muun muassa yrityksestä rekrytoida yhdysvaltalaisten teleyritysten työntekijöitä ja saada tätä kautta teknologisia tietoja.

Saatujen tietojen väitetään mahdollistaneen sen, että Huawei pystyi kehittämään samanlaisia tuotteita kuin kilpailijansa ja myymään niitä halvemmalla hinnalla.

Syyttäjien mukaan Huawei myös käynnisti sisäisen ohjelman, jossa tarjottiin bonuksia työntekijöille, jotka saivat haltuunsa teollisuussalaisuuksia kilpailijoita.

YHTIÖ KIISTI kaikki syytteet ja tyrmäsi tuomion. Huawean mukaan päätös on perusteeton, ja se kertoo aikeistaan ryhtyä oikeustoimiin.

Huawei on joutunut presidentti Donald Trumpin hallinnon silmätikuksi.

Hallinto on antanut ymmärtää, että valmistaja vakoilisi Kiinan valtion laskuun. Yhdysvallat on aiemmin varoittanut länsimaita olemaan käyttämättä Huawein infrastruktuuria uusien 5G-mobiiliverkkojen rakentamisessa.

title: Englanti on jo kansalaistaito – Suomi tarvitsee yhtenäisen kielipolun ja tuntijakouudistuksen
content:
Suomen kieltenopettajien liitto SUKOL ry vaatii päättäjiltä konkreettisia toimia kansallisen kielivarannon pelastamiseksi. Perusopetuksen tuntijako on uudistettava niin, etteivät vieraat kielet joudu kilpailemaan muiden valinnaisaineiden kanssa, ja kielten oppimisen jatkumo on turvattava varhaiskasvatuksesta korkeakouluihin.

Suomen kielitaitovaranto on kaventunut huolestuttavasti. SUKOL ry:n keräämät tilastot ja selvitykset osoittavat, että muiden vieraiden kielten kuin englannin opiskelu on vähentynyt kaikilla koulutusasteilla. Kuten SUKOL on johdonmukaisesti muistuttanut, pelkkä englannin kielen osaaminen ei enää riitä turvaamaan Suomen kansainvälistä kilpailukykyä, huoltovarmuutta, tutkimusta tai sivistysperustaa – Suomi tarvitsee kansallisen kielistrategian.

title: Sähkön hinta voi moninkertaistua hetkessä – maksuton Virtanen-palvelu auttaa
content:
Talvi lähestyy, ja sähkön hinnan voimakas vaihtelu tekee kulutuksen ajoittamisesta taas ajankohtaista. Vuonna 2026 pörssisähkön kuukausikeskihinta on vaihdellut rajusti: heinäkuun 1,93 sentistä helmikuun 17,22 senttiin kilowattitunnilta. Vuorokauden sisäinen vaihtelu on vielä suurempaa. Marraskuun 2026 alussa päivän halvimman ja kalleimman vartin hinnan ero oli melkein satakertainen.

Nitorin data-analyytikkojen kehittämä kaikille avoin, maksuton Virtanen.ai-työkalu auttaa kotitalouksia ymmärtämään, mihin sähköä todella kuluu. Uutuutena palvelussa voi nyt verrata pörssisähkön ja kiinteähintaisen sopimuksen eroja. Virtasella voi myös selvittää, onko noin vuosi sitten käyttöön otettu varttihinnoittelu tullut omassa taloudessa halvemmaksi vai kalliimmaksi.

”Sähkön hinta saattaa moninkertaistua hetkessä. Virtasen avulla voi laskea helposti, minkälainen sähkösopimus olisi tällä hetkellä oman kulutuksen kohdalla kaikkein järkevin”, palvelun kehittämisestä vastannut Nitorin data-asiantuntija Esa Puttonen kertoo.

title: Dear government, here's some money
content: If I could write a wishlist to the government, it’d be long. Dear government, free public transport for everyone, better education, and more support for cultural projects, please. They’d read it with a smile and a nod, then promptly tell me to give up. How are they supposed to pay for all that? State budgets across Europe are already under pressure. Luckily, I found a solution. Or at least the start of one. European banks are sitting on billions of euros in so-called dormant accounts. When people move abroad, or die without leaving any heirs or telling their heirs about their savings, their bank accounts are often forgotten and left untouched for decades. They become dormant assets – ghost money, if you will. In Germany, estimates for how much money is sitting in dormant accounts range from €4-9 billion. €9 billion! Currently, German banks pocket that money as their own income after 30 years, although if the owner somehow remembers their money later on, they can still claim it back. title: Israel/OPT: Women and girls bear the crushing toll of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza
content:
Israel has relentlessly inflicted repeated and cumulative harms on women and girls in the occupied Gaza Strip since October 2023 as an integral part of its ongoing genocide against Palestinians, said Amnesty International in a new report published today. 

No conditions for life: Women, girls and the gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, lays out in 135 pages of harrowing detail, Israel’s ongoing genocide despite the so-called ceasefire of October 2025, providing evidence of how the Israeli military, between 7 October 2023 and 1 October 2026, has repeatedly killed, injured, forcibly displaced, unlawfully detained, deliberately denied women and girls access to essential healthcare, including reproductive healthcare, and starved them. It illustrates how these measures have forced women into a daily struggle for survival defined by grief and trauma and stripped away the conditions necessary for women to exercise autonomy over decisions relating to pregnancy, childbirth and reproductive health.

title: Why is it getting so hard to watch football?
content: It's Champions League night. Nine matches are on the schedule. Millions of fans will tune in, some through paid streaming services, others via illegal websites. Either way, watching the beautiful game is getting increasingly complicated. If you've followed the competition for a few years, you probably remember when watching was much simpler. National broadcasters and telecom companies often held football rights and bundled matches into their TV, internet, and phone packages. That model is changing, said Thomas Peeters, a sports economist and professor at the Erasmus School of Economics. “A lot of the broadcasting rights that used to be free-to-air on one of the channels that you had anyway have been migrating to more streaming services dedicated specifically to sports.” In Germany, for example, DAZN shows all Champions League matches except the top match on Tuesday evenings, which Prime Video holds exclusively. In Italy, Sky shows most matches, and Prime Video again holds the rights to the top game on Wednesdays. title: CFP: BISA 2026: 20th Anniversary Conference
content:
Call for Papers

BISA 2026: 20th Anniversary Conference, Bristol

British and Irish Sound Archives (BISA) invites proposals for presentations at
this year’s BISA conference, which will be held at Bristol on Thursday 14 and
Friday 15 May 2026.

The two-day conference will feature presentations, practical sessions and
collaborative discussions, as well as the BISA Annual General Meeting.

We welcome proposals on any aspect of working in the sound heritage field. As
we will be celebrating our 20th anniversary in 2026, we’re interested in hearing
from archivists, engineers, researchers and other sound archives and creative
practitioners interested in reflecting on changes to practice, technology, and
research use that have taken place over the last two decades.

Previous delegates have also expressed an interest in the following aspects of
sound archive work and research: digitisation and digital preservation;
cataloguing; access and re-use; copyright and data protection; fundraising and
advocacy; and AI.

Please send a description of the presentation you propose, in no more than 300
words, to british.irish.sound.archive@gmail.com by 5pm on Friday 13 February.

title: Wikimedia Foundation Bulletin 2026 Issue 22
content:
Here is a quick overview of highlights from the Wikimedia Foundation since our last issue on November 6. Previous editions of this bulletin are on Meta. Let foundationbulletin@wikimedia.org know if you have any feedback or suggestions for improvement!

  • Thinking Beyond Pageviews: Traffic to Wikimedia sites is changing reflecting a rapidly changing internet ecosystem. We dig in deep to the pageview data to understand more thoroughly what is changing and how.
  • A place called “Home”: Home is designed to be a central place for Wikipedians at every stage, to find meaningful ways to participate and grow, through suggested edits (with a new task selection process), mentorship and impact. It was released as a Beta feature to 9 Wikipedias and will replace Special:Homepage at most of these wikis.
  • Collaborative embroidery Wikimania 2027: Submit a fabric square with your message about “The Internet we want”, which will be stitched into a larger tapestry inspired by the Chilean tradition of arpilleras. Find out how to participate in this historic Wikimedia movement-wide art project, regardless of whether you are traveling to Santiago in person.

title: Australian Billionaire Politician Clive Palmer and His Wanted Nephew Had Vanuatu Diplomatic Passports
content:
Australian billionaire politician Clive Palmer, along with his wife and nephew, received diplomatic passports and appointments from Vanuatu, according to a parliamentary report in the Pacific nation.

Vanuatu’s Public Accounts Committee recently released a report into the issuance of diplomatic passports by officials. Among more than two dozen cancelled diplomatic passports listed in an appendix to the report, OCCRP found Palmer and his two family members.

Palmer was appointed as a Vanuatu trade commissioner on May 29, 2023. Two months earlier, on March 17, Vanuatu gave a similar posting to his nephew, Clive Mensink — who was wanted by Australian authorities at the time for contempt of court in a case about a corporate collapse.

Palmer’s wife, Anna, was made a Vanuatu trade commissioner at the same time as her husband.

All three had their diplomatic passports cancelled in September of 2025, the appendix shows, as Vanuatu cracked down on the issuance of such documents to foreign and dual citizens.

“Mr. Palmer was invited to be an ambassador to the previous Vanuatu Government because of his experience in international trade,” said Andrew Crook, a spokesman for the billionaire.

title: How a Public Radio Project Turned the Public Domain Into a Creative Playground
content:
Simon Close says The Public Song Project invites people to think of the public domain as a free archive. It’s a place where creative works from the past can be adapted and reimagined through the eyes of new artists.

Close is a producer for WNYC public radio in New York City and host of the Public Song Project, now in its fourth year. The station partnered with the Internet Archive for the 2026 contest, which he said expanded the horizons of the project and helped boost entries to a new record surpassing 200 submissions.

“We’ve gotten some real experienced pros who make music their professional lives, and also people who came across the project and just like to be creative or have some emotional attachment to the song that they chose to cover,” Close said. “This year we had way more submissions from different parts of the country and, more thrilling, from all over the world.”

title: The speculative archaeologist
content:
Esin Karaosman, currently a Visiting PhD students at Linnaeus University, gave a research seminar entitled “‘We Are All (Speculative) Archaeologists’, Archaeological Imagination in the Making of Alternative Futures” for ten researchers attending the Higher Seminar in Cultural Sciences at Linnaeus University in Kalmar (24 November 2026).

She described the content of her presentation with these words:

How can an architect become a speculative archaeologist, conducting field research at the edge of knowledge and imagination? Archaeology has developed a way of knowing shaped by its encounters with material remains, where the instability, loss, and transformation of knowledge make imagination necessary. The presentation will explore “speculative archaeology” by reorienting this “archaeological imagination” toward alternative presents and futures. By treating knowing as a form of speculation, and therefore as a design problem, Esin investigates how we can stage encounters with what could be otherwise. She asks: If “we are all archaeologists,” can we also become speculative archaeologists in the making of alternative futures?

title: Kremlin Campaign to Crush Kaliningrad’s Identity
content:
Kaliningrad Regional Court sentenced lawyer and human rights defender Maria Bontsler to 12 years in prison for treason on November 12, after she was accused of passing information to Ukrainian intelligence. Bontsler’s real crime has been defending local people from political prosecutions.

The verdict was the latest step in a two-decade campaign to ensure Kaliningrad, Russia’s westernmost territory, has no independent political life.

For NATO planners, the exclave is a problem of missile ranges and the Suwałki Gap, the narrow strip on the border between Poland and Lithuania which links Kaliningrad to Belarus. For the Kremlin, weaponization of the territory is made easier by the absence of any civic movement that questions it.

It wasn’t always this way. Back in 1993, Sergey Pasko founded the Baltic Republican Party (BRP), which had influence beyond its list of barely 500 formal members.

title: Strengthening gender-inclusive mediation in an era of global uncertainty
content:
For three days, mediators, peacebuilding experts, diplomats and researchers from around the world gathered in Oslo to explore a pressing question: how can peace processes remain gender-inclusive and effective in an increasingly fragmented geopolitical landscape?

From 17–19 November, the UN High-Level Seminar on Gender and Inclusive Mediation Strategies brought together experts to share lessons, strengthen skills and examine current challenges facing peace mediation today.

Participants at the 15th UN High-Level Seminar on Gender and Peace Mediation Strategies in Oslo. PRIO / Cendi Frydenlund

Participants engaged in sessions covering gender-sensitive conflict analysis, mediation process design, conflict-related sexual violence, women’s participation in negotiations, peace agreement provisions and implementation challenges. The discussions took place against a backdrop of growing international tensions and increasing pressure on multilateral norms.

title: Sanctions against Russia are working, but shadow fleet and weapons’ production expose weaknesses
content:
Sanctions are having an effect, but their effectiveness is undermined by inconsistent enforcement, insufficient cooperation between countries and opportunities to circumvent the restrictions.

Why do gaps in the sanctions’ system persist, and what needs to change to ensure that sanctions achieve their intended goals? These questions were discussed by experts and representatives of national authorities at the Financial Intelligence Unit’s (FIU) eighth annual international sanctions conference, The Impact of Sanctions: Undermining Russia’s War Capabilities.

In October, the Council of the European Union adopted a decision to significantly expand its sanctions lists against Russia, imposing additional restrictive measures on more than 1,600 individuals and legal entities. This was the largest single expansion of individual EU sanctions imposed in response to Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine to date.

The sanctions targeted:

  • 826 companies;
  • 743 individuals;
  • 77 individuals involved in organising the illegal “elections”.

title: After COP31 setback, EU lawmakers greenlight carbon permit compromise
content:
A deal struck by EU negotiators in October has cleared its next hurdle, with the European Parliament voting to raise the threshold for cancelling surplus carbon permits from 400 to 700 million. The change aims to make the EU carbon market more flexible and predictable for industry.

The European Parliament approved on Tuesday changes to the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The agreement passed with 403 votes in favour, 78 against, and 146 abstentions.

Speaking ahead of the vote, Parliament’s rapporteur, MEP Pierfrancesco Maran (S&D/ITA), recalled the failure of COP31. It was, he noted, the first UN climate conference since 2009 to end without an agreement.

“Now, more than ever, Europe’s leadership is essential. But we are only credible if our ambition is matched by an effective instrument that transforms our economy. EU ETS is a good example of that,” he said.

Operating since 2019, the Market Stability Reserve absorbs surplus emission allowances and releases them when the market faces shortages. Under current rules, allowances held in the reserve above 400 million are permanently cancelled.

title: In Bulgaria, blood is a family affair
content: “When you pass by the hospital, a man will ask whether you need blood. In 2021, I paid 400 leva (€200) for a unit of blood,” said Hristo (not his real name) from Pernik, Bulgaria. Every day, around 600 Bulgarians need blood donations following accidents, surgeries, or chronic illnesses. Yet under Bulgarian law selling blood is illegal. In 2025, Bulgaria had 182,154 blood donors, according to Pencho Penchev, head of health policy at the Bulgarian Red Cross. That was an increase of about 2.5% from the previous year. Still, only 24 out of every 1,000 citizens donate blood. One reason for the shortfall is Bulgaria's so-called “family model”, under which patients rely on relatives to donate blood. These donations account for 85%-90% of the country's total blood supply. But what happens when you have a rare blood group and none of your relatives can donate? You go outside the hospital, where the dealer – often from the Roma community – offers to pose as a “relative” and donate his blood in exchange for a few hundred euros. “With rare blood types, you have no other choice” continued Hristo. title: A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon
content:
In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica.

The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record.

The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries.

If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.

title: Smartphones transform prison journalism. The FCC wants to jam them
content:
For most of society, the smartphone is just an ordinary part of modern life. But inside prisons like the one in Texas where I reside, that same technology fundamentally alters the balance of information and power.

Prison officials know this well, and they’ve collaborated with Brendan Carr’s Federal Communications Commission to allow cellphone jammers in state prisons. The FCC passed the initiative last week, although it’s up to states whether to participate.

Officials, of course, claim that the effort is needed to stop incarcerated people from coordinating crimes with those on the outside using contraband cellphones. But I strongly suspect that it’s really about censorship.

For the skeptical: Does anyone think those advocating for cellphone jamming would allow every incarcerated person a video camera instead of a cellphone? We all know the answer, and, if we’re being honest with ourselves, we know why.

The smartphone, labeled illegal contraband by prison officials, allows an incarcerated individual to completely circumvent institutional control designed to prevent those in its custody from accessing modern information ecosystems and documenting abuses.

title: Valtiota on vaikea rakentaa, ellei hoida ensin omia traumojaan, sanoo Rowda Olad
content:
Kun Rowda Olad palasi kotimaahansa Somaliaan vuonna 2016, hänellä oli suuria suunnitelmia. Hän aikoi perustaa maahan mielenterveysklinikan.  

Olad oli paennut maan sisällissotaa Yhdysvaltoihin lapsena ja mennyt yliopistoon. Pääaineeksi oli valikoitunut psykologia. Syynä oli se, että hän oli vieraillut Somaliassa muutamaa vuotta ennen paluutaan ja nähnyt, millä tolalla maan mielenterveyspalvelut olivat. 

Mielisairaaloita oli vain yksi, eikä sillä ollut riittävää kapasiteettia hoitaa potilaitaan. Monissa perheissä potilaat vain sidottiin paikalleen tai heitä yritettiin hoitaa perinteisten parannusmenetelmien avulla.

Maan olosuhteet olivat kuitenkin rauhoittuneet, ja Olad halusi osallistua valtion jälleenrakentamiseen avaamalla mielisairaalan.

”Sitten tajusin, ettei ammattilaisia ollut saatavilla eikä minulla olisi henkilökuntaa. Olen vain yksi ihminen. Sairaalan tai klinikan perustamisessa ei olisi järkeä.” 

Pian paluunsa jälkeen hän kiinnostuikin yksittäisten potilaiden hoitamisen sijaan siitä, miten mielenterveysongelmat vaikuttavat Somaliaan laajemmin: miten ne vaikeuttavat valtion instituutioiden rakentamista ja sisäisten konfliktien ratkaisemista.

title: Advancing M20 calls: Networks push EU on AI copyright and cloud safeguards
content:
Two global digital media networks have called on the European Union to include independent journalism in its push for digital sovereignty.

In two submissions to the European Commission in November, the EU is urged to confront Big Tech’s growing control over both the digital infrastructure journalists depend on and the news content AI companies use to build their products.

Together, the submissions argue that Europe’s digital sovereignty agenda must address both sides of the problem: who controls the infrastructure that delivers information;  and who controls — and profits from — the journalism that makes it valuable.

The submissions urge the EU to invest in independent, public-interest cloud infrastructure while strengthening copyright protections to prevent dominant AI companies from exploiting publishers’ work without fair compensation.

title: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar
content:
By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide.

The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted.

Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights.

Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya.
snippet: By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine

title: Diluted, abandoned...but it's not all bad news
content:
It’s six years since we got together with Climate Emergency UK to build CAPE, gathering together data on local councils’ climate commitments and plans.

Back then, we listed 328 councils who’d declared a climate emergency, and over the years we’ve kept up to date with which councils have published a plan and a date for reaching net zero, either in their own operations or across their region as a whole —
337 in all.

But times change, and the intervening years have seen some unexpected developments. It’s far from a straight line from a council making a climate pledge to reaching net zero carbon emissions, and we’ve seen target dates set back, pledges diluted, and in some cases, abandoned all together.

It's not all bad news, though: more councils have brought their net zero date forward or extended their ambitions than otherwise. It's a complicated picture — “a patchwork of commitments that create a postcode lottery on climate action”, as Climate Emergency UK’s Isaac Beevor says.

title: Can we play our way to better research data?
content:
Research data management and open science are important. But that does not mean they always have to be taught through another presentation, another checklist, or another hour of definitions.

What if researchers could solve a mystery, build with LEGO®, escape from a locked room, investigate persistent identifiers, or make decisions about the future of research data instead? There is a surprisingly creative world of games designed to do exactly that.

Many research data management topics are easier to understand when participants have to make decisions themselves.

  • Should this dataset be preserved?
  • Which metadata are actually necessary?
  • What happens when important information is missing?
  • Can this material legally be reused?
  • Which persistent identifier belongs to which research object?
  • And what consequences can today’s publishing decision have several years from now?
snippet: Research data management and open science are important. But that does not mean they always have to be taught through another presentation, another checklist, or another hour of definitions.

title: EU-komissiolta taloussapiskaa Suomelle
content:
EU-komissio patistaa Suomea ryhtymään kansallisessa budjettiprosessissaan toimiin sen varmistamiseksi, että Suomen vuoden 2027 finanssipolitiikka on EU:n taloussääntöjen mukaista.

Komission arvio perustuu Suomen alustavaan budjettisuunnitelmaan.

EU-komissio hyväksyi tiistaina talouspolitiikan EU-ohjausjakson syyspaketin. Komissio antoi lausunnot 17 euroalueen jäsenmaan alustavista vuoden 2027 talousarviosuunnitelmista.

Komissio arvioi, että Suomen lisäksi myös Saksan kohdalla on olemassa riski sääntöjen noudattamatta jättämisestä.

- Suomen ja Saksan kohdalla on riskinä, että ne jättävät noudattamatta nettomenojen enimmäiskasvuvauhtia, komissio kirjoittaa tiedotteessaan.

Hollannin, Kroatian, Liettuan, Luxemburgin, Maltan ja Slovenian näkymiä komissio piti Suomea ja Saksaa huonompana, sillä niiden kohdalla on komission mukaan olemassa riski sääntöjen merkittävästä noudattamatta jättämisestä.

SUOMI joutui viime talvena EU:n liiallisen alijäämän menettelyyn eli niin sanotusti talouden tarkkailuluokalle.

Menettely käynnistetään, jos jäsenmaan alijäämä ylittää kolme prosenttia suhteessa bruttokansantuotteeseen. Suomen alijäämä oli viime vuonna 3,4 prosenttia bruttokansantuotteesta.

title: Europe: Judgments on ‘instrumentalization’ of migration a devastating blow to the absolute prohibition of torture
content:
Today, the European Court of Human Rights ruled on cases of summary forced returns at the borders of Latvia, Lithuania and Poland with Belarus, also known as pushbacks, in cases of “instrumentalization of migration” defined by the Court as the actions of a state encouraging, facilitating or forcing migration with the aim of destabilizing another state.

The Court found that summary returns at the border in this context constitute a violation of the prohibition of torture only where applicants showed “evident personal vulnerabilities” or were able to demonstrate a real and immediate threat to life or risk of ill-treatment. Reacting to the judgments, Mandi Mudarikwa, Head of Strategic Litigation at Amnesty International said:

“These rulings strike a devastating blow to legal certainty and the protection of human rights at the borders under the European Convention of Human Rights. They limit the absolute protections guaranteed under the Convention only to people who are able to show evident vulnerabilities or that they are at immediate risk. This is despite the Convention entrenching such rights, such as the prohibition of torture, as absolute and the Court itself recognizing this fact.

title: CB Live: Carbon Brief journalists discuss key COP31 outcomes
content:
Following the close of COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, Carbon Brief’s journalists answered a range of questions in a CB Live panel discussion. 

COP31 came to a dramatic conclusion nearly 50 hours after its scheduled close – making it the longest COP in history. 

Less than 24 hours later, Carbon Brief published its 21,000-word summary, capturing everything that happened in the negotiations, the cover decision and more. 

This includes the “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, being rejected in the final hours of the summit by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations.

There was some progress at COP31, including an agreement on the adaptation fund, as well as a raft of announcements within the “action agenda”. 

Carbon Brief journalists – who followed every detail of the summit on the ground in Antalya and remotely answered a range of questions, including those sent ahead of time by CB+ members on CB Connect. 

These covered climate finance, China, the “just transition mechanism”, the potential for COP reform and much more.

title: How EPI-CATCH is teaching plants new tricks
content:
Plants have no brain, no nerves, and no ability to move away from danger. However, they can remember droughts, heatwaves, salinity, and other environmental stresses, and, in some cases, even pass those memories on to their offspring. Understanding how they do this was at the heart of the COST Action Epigenetic mechanisms of crop adaptation to climate change (EPI-CATCH).

The COST Action EPI-CATCH aimed to shed light on one of the most intriguing of these mechanisms: epigenetics. These biological processes enable plants to adjust to their environment without altering their DNA sequence. Over the course of four years, the Action brought together researchers from over 30 countries, trained a new generation of scientists, and produced knowledge that could help to develop climate-resilient crops for the future.

“We wanted to define, develop, and share new knowledge and methodologies for investigating epigenetic mechanisms involved in plant adaptation to environmental stresses driven by climate change,” says Prof. Federico Martinelli of the University of Florence, the Action Chair.

Did you know?

Some studies show that plants pass on epigenetic information better than animals

title: Showing up for Public Data: Our Gratitude
content:
For many of us, the Data Rescue Project was a lifeline over the past two years, giving us space and agency to work towards the future we wanted to see happen. This November, as many in America are preparing to celebrate Thanksgiving, we are grateful to every one of you for showing up. Truly. We've said it before, and we've said it again: the DRP community gave us hope during some of our darkest moments.

The recent blue wave in the US Midterms also bolsters us– it exceeded expectations and predictions, affirming that the voting public is unhappy with current elected officials and looking for change. However, that doesn't mean our work is done. Nearly all federal data is created under the executive branch, which has not changed hands. Federal data continues to be threatened, both in the short and long terms, so we need to continue showing up. 

We must carry on rescuing data and monitoring changes to these valuable resources. We have the responsibility to advocate for access to public data and build awareness among our community and users. And not least of all, we need to document the damage done for accountability and plan for a brighter and more sustainable future for federal data.

title: ICE Out of NJ Demands Freedom for Junior Marte & Other Former Delaney Hall Hunger Strikers
content:
Democracy Now! has obtained exclusive audio from inside Delaney Hall, the controversial immigrant detention center in Newark, New Jersey, operated by the for-profit prison company GEO Group. The audio was recorded over the summer during a labor and hunger strike organized by immigrant detainees. Junior Marte, an asylum seeker and father from Venezuela, was one of the organizers. He describes conditions inside the facility, including abusive treatment, medical neglect and prolonged legal limbo.

“We are here unjustly, wrongfully accused of being criminals. Yet immigration officials refuse to review our cases, because they know that we are all innocent people,” Marte says in the message.

The hunger and labor strike lasted for a month, with an estimated 300 detained immigrants participating in the protest. Jenny Garcia, campaign coordinator at the American Friends Service Committee of New Jersey, says that since the strikes, GEO Group and ICE have taken “every opportunity to retaliate against the strikers, the families visiting outside, and the protesters.”

title: ECHOLOT partners join AI campaign
content:
Two ECHOLOT partners have officially joined the ‘INNOVATE. PROTECT. EMPOWER: How cultural heritage can make Public AI a reality’ campaign, which was launched by the EU-funded European Heritage Hub at the end of September.

Read more about the INNOVATE.PROTECT.EMPOWER campaign.

The campaign, which is co-organised by Europeana (one of our ECHOLOT consortium partners), followed the publication of the European Heritage Hub’s policy paper entitled “Beyond adopter and supplier: putting cultural heritage at the heart of Europe’s Public AI ecosystem”. The paper highlights the cultural heritage sector’s role in the European Commission’s forthcoming AI strategy for the cultural and creative sectors, which is expected in 2027. The campaign translates its key messages into a call to action, inviting organisations and networks across Europe to endorse it.

ECHOLOT’s project coordinator, the Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology and University Library (TIB), has officially joined the campaign, thereby strengthening ECHOLOT’s presence alongside Europeana.

title: New York and California Age Gating Rules Go Into Effect in the New Year
content:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

title: Goat skin and indigo blue
content:
In CHARM, we have made a complete material analysis of a charter dated 19th August 1403, issued by Eric XIII of Pomerania and preserved in the town hall of Viipuri (Vyborg) – now at the National Archives of Finland. Erik of Pomerania (1381–1459) ruled the Kalmar Union from 1396 until 1439. In the charter, Eric grants the burghers of Viipuri the same urban privileges as those enjoyed by the city of Uppsala. 

ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) analysis identified that the parchment used for this charter was made from goatskin. This method identifies the animal species by analysing characteristic collagen peptides preserved in the material. Until now, we've mostly seen calfskin parchment used, therefore goat is a nice surprise!

Infrared (IR) imaging and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analysis provide clues about the ink used in the charter. The ink remains visible under infrared illumination, and XRF detected carbon, suggesting that the writing most likely is made with a carbon-based pigment.

title: Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home
content:
(Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch said today. The ICC trial in The Hague against Duterte for crimes against humanity is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts. Families of victims seeking to file new cases face significant barriers. Meanwhile, government records and human rights group reports show that drug-war abuses continue, with police harassing, arbitrarily arresting, and at times killing suspected drug dealers and users.

“President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.”

title: Quantum may be a bigger security risk than AI. Europe’s got a plan.
content:
BRUSSELS — As the world seeks a way through a wave of AI-powered cyberattacks and rogue agents, the next security threat already looms: quantum technology. 

With quantum computers set to break long-established protocols for securing digital information and communications in everything from messaging to banking services, their deployment in the next few years will spark a new security scramble.

The EU is hoping to get ahead of the risks with a Quantum Act rolling out Wednesday, which aims to secure the bloc’s digital infrastructure, according to a draft obtained by POLITICO.

Even as AI has helped to disrupt services from supermarket fridges to the European Commission’s own platforms over the past month, computer scientists contend that another, potentially more perilous moment for cybersecurity is on the horizon: Q-Day.

The fear is that quantum computers, which can process more than the classic 0s and 1s used by today’s machines, will eclipse current security vulnerabilities by breaking the standard methods of encryption that scramble information in order to lock it down — rendering everything from secure government systems to hospitals digitally defenseless.

title: Proteiiniomavaraisuus on kansallisen turvallisuuden kysymys – entiset kenraalit varoittavat EU:n ruokaturvan riskeistä
content:
Tänään julkaistu ympäristöjärjestö WePlanetin raportti tarkastelee ruoan ja rehun, erityisesti proteiinin, tuontiriippuvuutta EU:ssa ja siihen liittyviä geopoliittisia riskejä. Suomessa ja EU:ssa kehitetäänkin uusia menetelmiä, joilla proteiinia voidaan tuottaa.

Huoltovarmuuskeskus (HVK) totesi maaliskuussa 2026, että Suomen on vahvistettava omavaraisuuttaan kasviproteiinin tuotannossa. Luonnonvarakeskuksen selvityksiin perustuvan arvion mukaan Suomen proteiiniomavaraisuus on matalalla tasolla, mikä heikentää ruokajärjestelmän kriisinkestävyyttä.

Erityisen riippuvaista tuonnista on kotieläintuotanto, jossa tarvitaan runsaasti täydentävää valkuaisrehua. Pitkittyneessä kriisitilanteessa myös ihmisten ravinnoksi tarvittavasta proteiinista tulee pulaa, jos korvaaviin vaihtoehtoihin ei ole varauduttu.

Sama ongelma koskee koko Eurooppaa.

Raportin yhteydessä julkaistaan avoin kirje, jossa entiset kenraalit kehottavat EU:n päättäjiä suhtautumaan proteiinitarjonnan vakavien häiriöiden mahdollisuuteen turvallisuuspoliittisena kysymyksenä.

title: Telling Stories under Oppression: The Power of Textiles in Chile
content:
A powerful illustration of how stories can be told in empowering and engaging ways are arpilleras. Arpilleras are three-dimensional, hand-sewn appliquéd tapestries that “tell a story with each stitch”. They originated in Chile as a medium for women, generally working collectively, to denounce the human rights abuses and repression of the Pinochet dictatorship in Chile.

They have since been used to capture the first-person, lived experience of individuals and communities around the world, in response to war and conflict, and a wide range of other forms of oppression and social injustice.

title: UK Hacker Sentenced to Seven Years, Then Released
content:
British hacker Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced to seven years in prison on Monday for a series of cyberattacks targeting major international companies, but was released from custody the same day after the court took into account time he had already spent in detention.

Woolwich Crown Court initially imposed a nine-year sentence, reducing it by two years to reflect time Kurtaj had spent under a hospital order. He was subsequently released on license, meaning he remains subject to supervision and conditions.

Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group, pleaded guilty on November 16 to six offenses, including fraud, four violations of the Computer Misuse Act and illegally possessing a mobile phone in prison. Seven additional charges were left on file.

His attacks between 2020 and 2022 targeted companies including Uber, Revolut, telecommunications operators BT and EE, and Rockstar Games, the developer of the Grand Theft Auto franchise.

title: EU budget: Costa’s latest proposal fails to satisfy either side
content:
“I am convinced that this proposal is a good starting point for reaching a final agreement for three reasons. First, it is a budget that matches our ambitions. Second, it keeps national contributions within reasonable limits. Third, it includes a balanced basket of new own resources,” António Costa said.

The document is intended to break the deadlock among EU member states over the budget. The goal remains to reach an agreement before the end of 2026, allowing the necessary legislation to be adopted in 2027 and the new budget to take effect on January 1, 2028, according to the European Council.

Costa’s proposal has failed to meet the expectations of the so-called frugal countries — a group of net contributors to the EU budget that includes Germany, Austria, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and the Netherlands.

These countries are demanding significantly deeper spending cuts. They argue that the budget should focus more heavily on new priorities, above all defense and the competitiveness of the European economy, and devote less funding to traditional spending areas.

title: Europe is working more than ever, yet millions are still trapped in poverty. What does the EU advise?
content:
Despite record employment, the EU has cut the number of people at risk of poverty by less than a quarter of its 2030 target. The European Commission is urging governments to invest in people’s skills, create better jobs and strengthen competitiveness — while keeping public budgets in check.

The EU set its target in 2021, committing to lift at least 15 million people out of poverty or social exclusion by 2030 compared with 2019 levels. Until 2025, however, the number fell by just 3.5 million. With five years left, the bloc must make up remaining 11.5 million. That would require progress at roughly three times the pace achieved so far.

Meanwhile, higher energy prices are fuelling inflation, house prices continue to climb sharply across many member states, and borrowing costs are increasing. These are among the findings of the European Commission’s 2027 European Semester Autumn Package, presented on Tuesday, which sets out the bloc’s economic, social and employment priorities for the coming year.

While the EU is approaching its 2030 target of a 78 per cent employment rate, higher employment figures do not tell the whole story.

title: Surf's up, borders down
content: The ocean doesn't respect man-made borders, and the Curonian Spit – a 98-kilometre stretch between the coast of Lithuania and Russia's Kaliningrad region – is a perfect example. In the cold Baltic waters, surfers from both countries line up to catch the same waves, but they cannot cross from one side to the other. Between them lies a NATO-Russia border, along which Lithuania’s chief of defence recently suggested installing physical barriers to ensure continuous patrols. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Baltic Sea has become increasingly militarised and a stage for national military exercises. NATO has reinforced its maritime presence with warships, aircraft, and naval drones, while Russia maintains its Baltic Fleet in Kaliningrad. For Dima, surfer and member of Nida Surf Club on the Lithuanian side, nature makes these divisions look absurd. Both countries have the “same wind, same waves, same nature,” he tells The European Correspondent. title: At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix
content:
A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming.

Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause.

Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, reporting by Drilled and ProPublica has found.

title: Mother tongue language rights don’t implement themselves: Lessons from Nepal’s classrooms
content:
In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families.

“I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change.

For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom.

For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English.

Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue.

title: UN Womenin ja UNODC:n raportti: joka tunti viisi naista kuoli kumppaninsa tai lähisukulaisensa surmaamana vuonna 2025
content:
Kansainvälisen naisiin kohdistuvan väkivallan vastaisen päivän yhteydessä julkaistu vuoden 2026 katsaus naissurmiin, Femicide Brief 2026, osoittaa, että koti on edelleen naisille ja tytöille vaarallisin paikka. Tilanne ei ole juurikaan muuttunut vuosiin. Vuonna 2025 kaikista 78 000 naisiin ja tyttöihin kohdistuneesta sukupuoleen perustuvasta surmasta 60 prosenttia oli kumppanin tai perheenjäsenen tekemiä. Tämä tarkoittaa keskimäärin viittä surmattua naista tai tyttöä joka tunti – yhteensä 129:ää päivässä.

Naiset ja tytöt eivät ole turvassa naissurmilta missään päin maailmaa. Afrikassa kumppanin tai perheenjäsenen tekemien naisten ja tyttöjen surmien määrä suhteessa naisväestöön on korkein: 2,9 uhria 100 000 naista ja tyttöä kohden. Seuraavina tulevat Amerikka (1,4), Oseania (1,1), Aasia (0,6) ja Eurooppa (0,5).

”Olemme nähneet hälyttäviä tilastoja aivan liian pitkään”, sanoo UNODC:n pääjohtaja Monica Juma.

title: Pelastusylijohtaja vaaratiedotejärjestelmän testistä: ”Kokonaisuutta voidaan pitää onnistuneena”
content:
Tämänpäiväinen vaaratiedotejärjestelmän testi oli teknisesti onnistunut, sanoi pelastusylijohtaja Kimmo Kohvakka tiistaina sisäministeriön tiedotustilaisuudessa.

– Testaus sujui teknisesti suunnitellusti, kokonaisuutta voidaan pitää onnistuneena, Kohvakka sanoi.

Testin perusteella sekä FI-Alert-vaaratiedotejärjestelmä että 112 Suomi -sovellus toimivat, Kohvakka kertoi.

Kaikki eivät viestiä kuitenkaan edelleenkään saaneet. Tiedossa ei ole, kuinka monelta viesti jäi saamatta.

Kohvakan mukaan pelastuslaitosten kanssa tehtiin yhteistyötä, ja nopean ensihavainnon mukaan viestit menivät perille kohtuullisen kattavasti.

– Johtuen tästä tekniikasta on mahdotonta saada tarkkaa lukumäärää, koska tästä ei tule mitään tietoa lähettämispuolelle, Kohvakka sanoi viestien perillemenosta.

JÄRJESTELMÄÄ testattiin tiistaina puolenpäivän ja puoli yhden välillä. Testi antoi puhelimiin noin 10 sekunnin hälytysäänen sekä ilmoituksen, jossa kerrottiin kyseessä olevan vaaratiedotejärjestelmän kokeilu.

– Ilmoituksia on saattanut tulla vähän eri aikoihin eri päätelaitteisiin, sisäministeriön erityisasiantuntija Mikko Jääskeläinen sanoi tilaisuudessa.

title: University of Michigan Mailer Promises Its Data Center Isn’t Really a Data Center
content:
Over the past month, the University of Michigan sent postcards and pamphlets to people in Michigan telling them its new data center is “NOT a commercial data center” and is, instead, a “research computing center.”

According to one of the postcards viewed by 404 Media, the University’s data center will “advance breakthrough research in medicine, clean energy, cybersecurity, and engineering,” and "accelerate discoveries like new drug therapies and cancer treatments that improve people’s lives.” The University's postcard also promised to create 300 “high-quality union jobs during development” and “preserve approximately 80% of the 124-acre property as green space.”

One of U of M’s mailers said the building will not operate as a commercial data center. “This facility will not support streaming, entertainment, social media, or e-commerce,” it said. It also said the facility will not “burden the local community with the cost of its energy or water use, drain resources from the local community or raise utility rates,” or “create smoke, odors, or significant noise.”

title: Egypt: Authorities must reverse decision to close Mada Masr and drop all charges against its editor in chief Lina Attalah
content:
Ahead of an appeal hearing on 25 November against the closure of Mada Masr and the conviction of its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah for operating a website without a license Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Sara Hashash, said:

“Egyptian authorities have an opportunity to change course and meet their international obligations by reversing this disgraceful decision to shut down Mada Masr. The latest escalation against Mada Masr is a chilling signal of the Egyptian authorities’ resolve to silence independent journalism and eradicate any critical reporting that challenges the official narrative or scrutinizes their human rights record or other conduct. Egyptian authorities must immediately end their brazen assault on press freedom, quash the closure order against Mada Masr– one of the few remaining lifelines for independent information about Egypt.

“The authorities should also drop all charges against Lina Attalah who faces trial in a separate case, on charges of publishing false news and operating a website without a licence, for which she could be sentenced to up to one year in prison.

title: COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya
content:
The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, failed to agree on a “pact” that – despite making no clear reference to fossil fuels or adaptation finance – had contained strong signals for oceans.

The “Antalya pact” took up much of the two weeks of negotiating time in Turkey, only to be rejected during the closing plenary by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable countries.

Several countries expressed their regret during the plenary that significant work on advancing ocean-climate action would be lost.

The COP ran nearly 50 hours over time, but did not end with substantive outcomes on several key topics.

For the second year in a row, negotiations on agriculture and food security broke down and will now have to resume next year.

Food-systems advocates were, however, heartened by the explicit inclusion of “agroecology” in a decision within the “just transition work programme”. 

Ocean-conservation groups noted an increased focus on ocean-climate links at this year’s COP, but said COP31 did not live up to its promise of being a “blue COP”.
snippet: The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, failed to agree on a “pact” that – despite making no clear reference to fossil fuels or adaptation finance – had contained strong signals for oceans.

title: "Only Path Forward Is to Abolish": Outcry After Masked ICE Agents Arrest Family at Seattle Airport
content:
Washington Governor Bob Ferguson and other officials in the state have denounced the violent arrest of a father and daughter by ICE agents on Saturday as they were boarding a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Video of the arrest shows masked plainclothes agents dragging a woman off the jetway as she screams for help. Both Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle said ICE carried out the operation without their knowledge. ICE said Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, originally from Mexico, was targeted for overstaying his tourist visa, and that his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, would be charged with assault for allegedly throwing hot coffee at an agent — although witnesses dispute that account.

“This is one of, unfortunately, many thousands of detentions that is happening not only in Washington state, but across the country,” says Josefina Mora-Cheung, director of organizing for the immigrant justice group La Resistencia. “The only path forward is to abolish ICE.”

title: Signal Moves to Block AI Agents
content:
Signal announced an update to its mobile apps on iOS and Android that seeks to curb issues with AI agents accessing private chats. This is a useful new barrier against a problem we’ve been highlighting this year in our Encrypt It Already campaign. And good news, it’s enabled by default so you don’t need to do anything except update the app.

Over the last year, both Google and Apple* have released AI features in their operating systems that can read the contents of apps. One of the ways it can do this is through screen analysis. Google calls this feature “Intelligent Screen Context,” while Apple refers to it as either “Onscreen Awareness” or “Visual Intelligence.”

title: Pakistani Prisoners Face Poor Access to Health Care
content:
When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.

Human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care. Many inmates who fall ill in custody fail to receive prompt or decent care at all.

After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.

title: Marie Curie Became the First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize, the First Person to Win Twice, and the Only Person in History to Win in Two Different Sciences
content:
For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes.

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “Floating University” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

title: Snowden on steroids: AI agents in phones trigger surveillance fears
content:
AI agents are lurking in your phone, hoovering up your messages, pictures and emails in a privacy breach that “makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke,” privacy proponents are warning.

Privacy-preserving messaging app Signal has started blocking screenshots by default in an attempt to stop AI agents from reading people’s screens and capturing potentially sensitive data.

The makers behind Signal — which is considered the industry gold standard for confidential, encrypted messaging — warned that Google, Apple and Microsoft are integrating autonomous agents “deep” within their device operating systems, allowing the agents to bypass privacy safeguards in individual apps.

“The ability for billions of devices to permanently spy on their users makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke,” Udbhav Tiwari, head of strategy and global affairs at Signal, told POLITICO, referring to the 2013 disclosures about mass U.S. government surveillance.

Tiwari warned that governments with a penchant for surveillance could ask tech firms for access to data gathered by AI agents, skipping the need to break end-to-end encryption or install malware on someone’s device.

title: Wikidata Reference Validator Tool: Improving Verifiability Across Wikidata
content: Wikidata depends on reliable, verifiable references to maintain trust across its open knowledge base. During the Wiki Indaba 2026 Hackathon, our team worked on Project 04 under the Verification and Consistency track, mentored by Josef Anthony and Birusha. Together, we updated the Wikidata Reference Validator Tool, a dedicated utility designed to check references, identify broken links, and help editors maintain the reliability and verifiability of information on Wikidata. The core issue our team set out to tackle is the presence of broken or outdated external references on Wikidata. While some references remain fully accessible and work correctly, others are completely broken because the links no longer work and return 404 errors. Another major challenge comes from outdated links, where a page still exists online but contains old or no longer maintained information. These broken and outdated references undermine the reliability of the platform by making it much harder to verify information, which is why identifying them automatically is critical to improving Wikidata verifiability.

title: European Parts Made in 2026 Found in Russian Drones
content:
European electronic components manufactured as recently as February 2026 have been found in Russian drones used against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, highlighting Russia's continued access to foreign technology despite years of Western sanctions.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office said investigators have identified more than 16,000 foreign-made components in Russian drones, missiles and other weapons — the highest figure reported by Ukrainian authorities to date.

“Based on inspections of incident sites, expert examinations and analysis of physical evidence, more than 16,000 foreign-made components have been identified so far,” the office told OCCRP and its partners, the Kyiv Independent, De Tijd and Paper Trail Media. 

“These components are used in drones, missiles and other weapons in service with the aggressor state [Russia] (…) and bear the markings of companies from over 30 countries,” it said.

Ukraine's military intelligence has published details of more than 6,300 foreign-made components found in Russian weapons on its War & Sanctions website.

title: Life on the Edge of War: Are Poland and South Korea Safe?
content:
From the perspective of someone living in South Korea and observing the reality firsthand, the similarities in how people in both countries perceive security are striking  On one hand, life proceeds under the shadow of geopolitical struggles. In Poland, it is the war in Ukraine; in South Korea, it is the threat posed by a neighbouring country with which no peace treaty has been signed.

On the other hand, both societies face unexpected threats occurring on their own streets. Recently, both countries have witnessed terrorist attacks on civilian populations. These had devastating effects on the sense of security across both nations.

However, on-the-ground interviews conducted with South Koreans specifically for FocusEurope.pl, show that they have much more in common with their Polish counterparts. They seem remarkably adept at adapting to persistent threats .

In Seoul, you can walk home late or catch a cab without worrying whether the trip will be safe. The same goes for leaving your phone at the table while going to the restroom. People don’t automatically assume that someone will rob or take advantage of them.

title: Electric cars pull ahead. Brussels puts brakes on imported hybrids
content:
Europeans are buying electric cars at record speed. Yet Brussels is busy protecting a different technology. From December, the EU will cap imports of hybrid cars, while lawmakers consider keeping hybrids and combustion engines on sale after 2035.

For many drivers, the maths has changed. A home-charged electric car now costs about half as much to run as a petrol or diesel one, according to the green group Transport & Environment (T&E). Cheaper models are arriving too. T&E expects sales of electric cars under €25,000 to rise sevenfold this year compared with 2024.

The shift shows in the latest figures. Between January and October, almost one in four new cars registered in the EU ran on batteries alone, the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) reported on Tuesday. Electric cars also outsold petrol models over the period. Hybrids, however, remain the most popular choice.

title: Field notes from a failed COP31
content: Friday evening, the official final day of the COP31 climate negotiations. Standing on a chair with a red noose around his neck, Malaysian activist Amalen Sathananthar shouts: “You are killing the future! Why don’t you just kill me now?” It took two additional days – almost 50 hours into overtime – for delegates to give up. The EU and others rejected the final draft because it left out the two words at the root of the climate crisis: fossil fuels. They disappeared under pressure from Saudi Arabia and the Arab Group, backed by a bloc of like-minded developing countries, opposed to any mention of fossil fuels or “top-down” targets. The text “does not begin to address the climate emergency we face,” said Irish minister Darragh O'Brien. “The EU cannot accept it.” His words were met with applause. What is now the longest COP on record, is the first since 2009 to end without an overarching agreement. But this may not be the worst possible outcome. “This collapse is better than a half-hearted final document would have been,” said Johan Rockstrom and Ottmar Edenhofer from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
content:
Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.

In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission.

A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.

Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.”

“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.

title: Trump had 4 reasons to ‘convince’ Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang. Here’s why it matters globally
content:
Just 11 days after resigning as chip maker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang has been rehired by the company he co-founded, vowing “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around”.

The company’s board said its unexpected, unanimous decision came after “input from senior levels of the United States government”.

US President Donald Trump went even further, declaring in an interview that he “convinced them” to bring Huang back. The company had bluntly ruled out Huang’s return just days ago.

But why would a US president meddle so openly in the world’s second-most valuable company? And why does the leader of Nvidia matter beyond the US – including the speed at which data centres are built worldwide?

Nvidia’s stocks plunged after Huang announced his resignation on November 12, following reports of extramarital affairs, one with a woman identified by US intelligence as being in touch with China’s top spy agency and another with an Nvidia employee. Both raised concerns about Huang’s judgement as CEO.
snippet: Just 11 days after resigning as chip maker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang has been rehired by the company he co-founded, vowing “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around”.

title: Kaupan liitot huolestuivat vaalitavoitteista – PAM: Emme tähtää osa-aikatyön kieltämiseen
content:
Kaupan liitto ja Erikoiskaupan liitto ovat huolissaan SAK:n ja PAMin osa-aikatyötä koskevista vaalitavoitteista. PAM rauhoittelee etujärjestöjä, että ammattiliitto ei halua kieltää osa-aikatyötä.

Kaupan ja Erikoiskaupan liitot kertoivat huolistaan palkansaajajärjestöjen osa-aikatyölinjauksista eilen. Niiden arvion mukaan ehdotukset vaikeuttaisivat osa-aikatyön tarjoamista tai lisäisivät sen kustannuksia. Liitot korostavat, että ehdotuksia on arvioitava myös niiden työllisyysvaikutusten näkökulmasta.

– Osa-aikatyön merkitys on ymmärrettävä laajemmin. Osa-aikatyötä ei pidä arvioida ainoastaan sen perusteella, kuinka moni haluaisi enemmän työtunteja, vaan myös sen perusteella, kuinka monelle se mahdollistaa työn tekemisen, Kaupan liiton työmarkkinajohtaja Anna Lavikkala sanoo tiedotteessa.

Suomen ammattiliittojen keskusjärjestö SAK ja Palvelualojen ammattiliitto PAM esittävät vaalitavoitteissaan muun muassa, että osa-aikatyölle vaadittaisiin perusteet. Työnantajan velvollisuutta tarjota kokoaikatyötä osa-aikatyötä tekeville työntekijöille on SAK:n mukaan vahvistettava.

title: Ethiopia: Lethal artillery strikes on civilian neighbourhoods in Tigray’s Alamata city must be investigated as war crimes
content:
Artillery attacks by Ethiopia’s military and its allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) that killed dozens of civilians and injured many more in the city of Alamata in the northern region of Tigray, between 26 and 28 September, must be investigated as possible war crimes, Amnesty International said today.

The organization also found that forces affiliated to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), put civilians in harm’s way by establishing military bases in populated residential areas, including in several schools in Alamata, prior to the outbreak of renewed fighting in the region.

The Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) and its TPF allies seized control of the strategic city of Alamata, a key supply hub for troops, food, and fuel, from the TPLF on 28 September.

title: Too Big to Fire? Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia; Questions Loom Over AI Boom & U.S.-China Relations
content:
Nvidia stock prices surged over 30% on Monday as the chip maker reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Huang had stepped down earlier in November amid reports he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of spying for China. Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI boom, and the leadership turmoil had erased trillions in value from the U.S. stock market. President Donald Trump acknowledged he had encouraged the company’s board to bring Huang back.

“The fact that our markets are so over-indexed on the AI trade, that something like three-fourths of gains in the [S&P 500] this past year have been AI-related, is unsustainable,” says Aya Ibrahim, senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute.

We also speak with organizer and researcher Tobita Chow, who says Huang’s “spy scandal” that led to his ouster is part of a larger effort by anti-China figures in the U.S. national security establishment to escalate tensions between the countries.

title: EU: Forced Labor Remedies Should Center on Workers
content:
(Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions said in a report released today. 

In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

“Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” said Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”
